extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and typesetters preparing manuscripts for The University of Chicago Press (or similar book publishers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for manuscript preparation, typographic spacing and indentation, headings and proofs, and operational practices for authors, editors, proofreaders, and copyholders working on book production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin space after symbols and before certain abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, ^, and similar signs; before "f.," "ff.," and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "§14.     Be it further ordained . . . ."; pp. 10 ff.; 16 cm.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between monetary symbols and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols, $ and £ (pounds), s. (shillings) and d. (pence), and the numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $2.75; £10 5s. 2d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at line-beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic numerals at the beginning of lines, denoting subsections, there should be an en-quad; after Roman numerals, an em-quad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Roman numerals in cap, cap-and-small-cap, or small-cap center-heads there should be an em-quad. Small-cap headings should have an en-quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing in scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced in the specified manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing in algebraic/products and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (as printed): Ai v' = 2m^ {v^z^ — 2vwyz -+- 2'w^y').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation by measure and type size
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify indentation amounts (in ems or points) depending on measure (pica width) and type size for plain paragraphs and hanging indentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of 10–20 picas, ii-pt., 1 em; lo-pt., i¼; 9-pt., i; 8-pt., i¼; 6-pt., 2. Detailed tables given for ranges 10–20 and 20–30 and for hanging indentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Center the longest line and govern indentation of other lines by it; where longest line is disproportionately long, strike an average of long lines. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines; align blank verse and consecutive rhymes; indent alternate rhymes alike; indent disproportionately short lines more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quotations from different poems in succession vary slightly in line length, indent all alike. Example guidance and multiple illustrative poetic excerpts are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hanging indention chiefly to bring into relief the opening word(s) of a paragraph, a number introducing such paragraph, or when a center-head makes more than three lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of leads and leaded/solid setting
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary standard lead is 2 points. Matter with leads between the lines is called leaded; without, solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly all books are set leaded. The Manual itself is set leaded, with certain paragraphs (like the Index) set solid as illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of slugs and standard sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: A slug is a strip of metal thicker than a lead used in make-up of printed matter; two standard sizes are 6 and 12 points (a nonpareil and a pica) thick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-head rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed at equal distances from both margins; center-heads are usually set in caps or in small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a center-head makes more than one line, use the (inverted) 'pyramid' form for two or three lines, or 'hanging indention' for more than three lines. Example: SEC. VII. THE PRINCIPLES OF SOCIOLOGY

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page or column; it may be set in a separate line (flush) or run in with the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The run-in form is more common. Side-heads are most frequently set in italics; sometimes in caps and small caps or in bold-face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-in-head definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually set in different type and as a rule placed under the first two lines of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example paragraph demonstrates placement under first two lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box-head and running-head definitions and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table. A running-head is a headline placed at the top of each page, usually giving the main title on the verso and chapter title on the recto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running-heads should be set in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph types (plain vs hanging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of paragraphs are distinguished — plain and hanging. A plain (regular) paragraph has the first line indented and the others set flush. A hanging paragraph has the first line set flush and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples and cross-references to headings are provided (see also hanging indention guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of proofs (galley/page/plate/foul/revise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galley-proof, page-proof, plate-proof (foundry-proof), foul proof, and revise are defined with their usage in the production process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plate-proofs have a black border and many publications are printed from such plates. A foul proof is a galley-proof containing author's corrections. A revise is a new proof corrected from a marked proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up and folio conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make-up is arranging into page-form of type-lines. Folio conventions: even numbers on verso, odd on recto; drop-folio is a page-number at the bottom. A half-title or bastard title is the abbreviated title on a separate page preceding the full title-page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscripts should be typewritten or clearly handwritten
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be either typewritten or in a perfectly clear handwriting; typewritten is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheets should be uniform size (9"x11" desirable); use only one side; never roll manuscripts; place flatly in a box or envelope; sheets should not be fastened except by pins or clips that can be removed; when fastening one piece to another use mucilage, not pins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave liberal margins and number pages consecutively
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberal margins should be left at the top and left-hand side for reader/printer directions. Pages should be numbered consecutively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inserted and omitted pages should be clearly indicated (e.g., sheets to be inserted after p. 4 marked '4A','4B'; omitted pages indicated by numbering p. 4, '4-7'). Additions placed after the sheets to which they belong should be marked 'Insert A', etc., with insertion points noted in original margins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph marking in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated, either by indenting the first line or by a ^ mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote presentation and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes should be clearly designated (separate line or different ink). The word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number footnotes consecutively throughout an article or by chapters; note that in hot-type (linotype) the slightest change may necessitate resetting whole lines, so renumbering can be expensive. This difficulty is not met in monotype or hand-set matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit copy for title-pages, prefaces, tables, and indexes with manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy for title-pages, prefaces, tables of contents, etc., should be submitted with the manuscript. Copy for indexes should be compiled from the special set of page-proofs furnished and promptly delivered to the printers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary delay is often caused by postponing these details till the last minute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and return proofs promptly and use standard marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets, use the standard proofreaders' marks; do not adopt a system of your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs. Delays and errors often result from not attending to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize changes and avoid plate corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that changes in the type cost money; make manuscripts as perfect as possible before delivering to the printer. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided as they are expensive and apt to injure the plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alterations should be made in the galley-proof; each succeeding stage adds to the cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return original manuscript with proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The original manuscript should be returned with the galley-proof so the proofreader may refer to it and each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assists in calculating alteration costs properly chargeable to the author/editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreaders: read as the author and be the judge of correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread everything as if you yourself were the author; be particularly careful about proper names and figures; if copy is not clear investigate or query the author. Do not follow copy blindly; follow copy only when, and as far as, it is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never hesitate to correct anything palpably wrong even if copy asserts the contrary; the proofreader will bear the blame for errors left uncorrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreader professional conduct and queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Make queries clear and transferred to proofs; be discreet, avoid trivial criticisms, and learn the 'personal equation' of editors you work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ask authors or editors to decide questions of style; the Manual of Style is primarily meant for the proofreader. If rushed beyond reasonable limits, state that you have done your best and disclaim further responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put initials on every galley you read or revise
rubrics_metrics.description: Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This saves time tracing proofs and ensures credit is given where due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholders: reading technique and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading-voice; ensure small words are read as carefully as big ones; enunciate plural 's' distinctly; regulate and equalize speed; do not guess at words; sit at right angles to reader; slow when reader marks corrections; evolve a private system of signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not waste time on matters of style (the proofreader is supposed to know the rules); be careful transferring marks; in sending out proofs ensure everything is there; manuscript should accompany galley-proof; indicate envelope contents; fasten pins center at top; return reference volumes to file each evening; keep proofroom neat and orderly and maintain records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard proofreader's marks (symbols and meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the standard, conventional proofreader's marks rather than inventing idiosyncratic symbols; the manual lists common marks and their intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the list: Put in SMALL CAPITALS (Capitals), put in lower case (l.c.), put in roman type (rom.), put in italics (ital.), put in bold-face type (bold-face), delete (˂§), letter reversed — turn, indent / make a new paragraph (D/ ^), put in space (|:), close up (3), bad spacing — space more evenly (Y(\), wrong font/character of wrong size (i.), transpose (trsp.), carry left/right (←, →), elevate/depress (↑/↓), perfect letter (X), shove down (space shows between words), straighten crooked line, restore words crossed out, print as a logotype, indicate words omitted, query to author (?).
